I was proud, I was content. Then I met you. And my craft was no longer enough.”

I wanted to capture not your likeness, which is the painter’s trade, but your essence. I wanted to distil the music that I alone seemed to hear when you entered a room; the particular melody of your youth, your laughter, your inimitable grace. The thought took hold of me like a fever. It became an obsession. For a year, every other commission was a burden, every other task a drudgery. My life narrowed to that one object, to the little box of satinwood and silver that now sits in that cabinet.”

“I laboured as I have never laboured before. I melted down silver from an old Florentine chalice to cast the tiny figures. I spent a month in the Black Forest, not to find a cuckoo for a clock, but to find a man who could teach me the forgotten art of tempering bell-steel to produce a tone of unearthly purity. Every gear was cut by my own hand, not to a measurement from a book, but to a feeling, a rhythm that I felt was yours. I was not merely an artisan, Julian; I was an alchemist. I was trying to transmute base metal not into gold, but into a soul.”

He finally turned, and his eyes, full of a terrible, devoted sadness, met Julian’s. “The melody it plays… it is not something I composed in the ordinary sense. It came to me in a dream, a dream in which you were speaking, and your words were not words, but notes of music, clear and perfect and heartbreakingly pure. When I awoke, I wrote it down, and I knew I had it. I had the music of your being. To build that box, to give that melody a physical voice, was the one great artistic act of my life. I poured all of my skill, all of my adoration, all of myself into it. When it was finished, I was finished, too. I had nothing left to give. My genius, if I ever possessed such a thing, is locked away inside it, with the ghost of that melody. To attempt to make another would be a sacrilege. It would be like a priest trying to celebrate a second Mass with an empty chalice. There is nothing there. You have it all. That is my secret, Julian. The utter, devastating emptiness of my own art. Now, tell me yours.”

A pang of pity, sharp and unwelcome, pierced Julian. For a moment, he saw the man before him not as a nuisance or a threat, but as he truly was: a creator utterly enslaved by his own creation, a worshipper kneeling before an empty altar. The tragic sincerity of the confession was almost beautiful. It was a work of art in itself. But pity was a useless emotion, a sentimentalist’s indulgence. And besides, his own danger was far too pressing. The musician’s confession, in its pathetic splendour, had not cornered him; it had given him his weapon.

A slow smile of relief, of dawning triumph, touched Julian’s lips. He stepped forward, his entire demeanour changed. The petulance and terror were gone, replaced by a soft, almost tender gravity.

“Alistair,” he said, and his voice was a balm, “that was the most beautiful, the most terrible confession I have ever heard. I feel as if I have been allowed to look into the very heart of a saint. You put your soul into my music box. You say your very genius is contained within it.”

“It is the truth,” Alistair whispered, bewildered by the change in the young man.

“I know it is,” Julian continued, his voice resonating with a newfound, persuasive warmth. “I have always known it. I have felt it. And now you see, don’t you? Now you must understand why I cannot allow anyone to see it, why I keep it hidden away. It is not for my sake, Alistair. It is for yours.”

The musician stared at him, his brow furrowed in confusion. “For mine?”

“Of course! You, its creator, would profane it? You would take this… this reliquary of your own spirit, this testament to an adoration you call devastating, and you would write a paper about it? For the Horological Society? You would speak to them of its ‘unique escapement’? You would hand over your soul for them to measure with calipers and praise with their dry, technical jargon? You would allow men who see only gears and levers to peer into the mechanism that holds the very music of your being? It would be a vivisection. A desecration of the highest order. I am not hiding the box, my dear, dear friend. I am protecting it. I am protecting you. I am keeping your great secret, the one you have just confessed to me, safe from the vulgar eyes of the world.”

He delivered the words with such passionate conviction that he almost believed them himself. He saw the logic of his argument reflected, dawning, in Alistair’s astonished eyes. The musician was a man of art and sentiment; to appeal to the sanctity of his creation was to strike the one note he could not resist.

Alistair was staggered. He looked from Julian’s earnest, beautiful face to the cabinet in the corner and back again. The boy’s argument was an exquisite piece of sophistry, a perfect inversion of the truth, and yet, in his emotionally flayed state, it seemed to possess an unassailable logic. Had he been about to commit such a vulgarity? To reduce his life’s great passion to a mere technical curiosity for a professional journal? The thought now seemed monstrous to him. Julian, in his youthful, almost divine sensitivity, had understood the truth of the matter better than he had himself. His desire to hide the box was not selfishness; it was an act of profound artistic reverence.

“Julian,” he stammered, “I… I had not seen it like that. You are right. Of course you are right. It would be a profanation. Forgive me. I have been blind. My pride in the mechanism, my foolish, craftsman’s vanity… it obscured the truth.” He passed a hand over his weary eyes. “To think I was angry with you. You were only being the perfect guardian of my work. Of my… soul.”

“Then you will not write the article?” Julian asked softly, pressing his advantage.

“Never. I swear it. No one shall ever know of its construction from me. It will remain what it is: a mystery. Our mystery.”

“Our mystery,” Julian repeated, and the words were like the closing of a lock. “And you understand, then, why you cannot look at it? To see it now, after this, would be to reduce it back to a mere object. Let it exist for both of us as it should: a perfect memory. A perfect work of art. He had offered his soul and, in a way he could not quite fathom, it had been accepted and enshrined. He picked up his hat and gloves from the chair where he had thrown them. “I should go. “I know,” said Alistair with a sad smile. He paused at the door, his hand on the knob, and looked back at Julian, whose beauty in that moment seemed to him more radiant, more astonishing than ever. “Keep it safe, Julian. Keep our secret safe.”

“I will guard it with my life,” Julian said, his expression one of perfect sincerity.

A profound sense of relief washed over him, so potent it was almost a physical pleasure. He had been on the very edge of the abyss, and he had pulled back, not by force, but by a delicate, artistic lie. He had played upon the man’s soul as if it were a rare and sensitive instrument. Caspian would have been proud.

He walked over to the cabinet, his heart beating a little too quickly. He drew the small, ornate key from his waistcoat pocket, the very key Alistair had so nearly demanded. He unlocked the inlaid door and there it was, resting on a bed of dark velvet. The satinwood box, inlaid with threads of silver and mother-of-pearl, seemed to glow with a soft light of its own. It was a masterpiece, a thing of flawless and absolute beauty. On the outside.

With a trembling finger, Julian pressed the hidden catch. The lid sprang open. For a moment, there was silence. Then, the mechanism whirred, and the music began.

But it was not the music Alistair had described. It was not the melody of his youth, clear and perfect and pure. The theme was there, recognizable in its bones, but it was horribly changed. It was as if a beautiful face had been afflicted with some creeping, disfiguring disease. The tempo was frantic, hurried, and the notes, once so crystalline, now possessed a jarring, metallic quality. A sour, flat note repeated itself where a clear, high tone should have been. The delicate harmonies had become a jangling, hurried discord, a melody gone mad, stumbling over itself in its haste to finish. It was the music of a panicking, corrupted soul. It was the sound of his own damnation, rendered in clockwork and steel.

A wave of nausea and terror swept over him. He slammed the lid shut, cutting off the grotesque parody of a tune. The sudden silence was a mercy. He leaned his head against the cool wood of the cabinet, his body trembling. Alistair’s confession had been more true than the poor man could ever imagine. His soul was indeed in that box, but it was his own, Julian’s, that was providing the terrible, discordant music. Each selfish act, each cruel word, each moment of moral decay, twisted the delicate mechanism, bent the tines of the comb, and turned the melody uglier. He had told Alistair he would guard it with his life. He had spoken the literal truth. Its secret was the secret of his life, and the cost of its preservation was the slow, inexorable ruin of his own spirit. He was, as Caspian had so often advised, the spectator of his own life; he had not realized that the spectacle would be a horror show, and the price of admission was everything he had once been. He locked the cabinet again, and turning away, caught a glimpse of his own face in a mirror. It was untroubled, beautiful, and smiling.
